source.title: UQABench: Evaluating User Embedding for Prompting LLMs in Personalized Question Answering
source.authors: Langming Liu; Shilei Liu; Yujin Yuan; Yi-Zhe Zhang; Ben-Cheng Yan; Zhi-Yuan Zeng; Zihao Wang; Jiaqi Liu; Di Wang; Wen-Bo Su; Peng-Jie Wang; Jian Xu; Bo Zheng

record.file_problem: The paper text is complete. The ACM citation and conference details contain template placeholders.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates scaling of user-encoder models in personalized question answering, a different setting and measure from language-model pretraining-loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study's scaling experiments vary user-encoder parameter count and interaction-sequence length, and report downstream task scores. They do not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, training compute, compute-optimal allocation, or extrapolation of language-model loss. Only V6 is tested here, through downstream performance across user-encoder sizes. The sequence-length sweep is not a test of the claim's training-token scaling.
record.test_reason: The study scales a Transformer user encoder (Trm++) from 3.2M to 1.2B parameters, with Qwen2.5-3b-instruct fixed, and reports downstream personalized-Q&A accuracy at each size plus a fitted log-linear trend. This is a new setting for V6: downstream performance against scale, but for a recommendation-sequence encoder prompting an LLM rather than for language models themselves. No pretraining loss is reported, so V1, V2, V3, V5 and V7 cannot be assessed.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors report a clear scaling law between encoder size and personalized-Q&A performance, fitted as log-linear in parameter count. They also report that longer pretraining sequence length helps, with diminishing gains beyond about 256.
record.recipe_differences: Scales user recommendation encoders and measures personalized-Q&A task scores, rather than scaling language models and measuring held-out pretraining loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Encoder parameter count and pretraining sequence length are varied. The authors also report that Q-Former fine-tuning is sensitive to hyperparameters such as learning rate and can produce NaN loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Performance rises with the pretraining interaction-sequence length of the encoder (avg 33.38 at 32 to 53.88 at 512), with diminishing gains beyond 256. IP dips from 69.33 to 68.71 at 512 (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance of sequence encoders improves with input context length, with diminishing returns.

record.peer_reviewed: Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (2025), as provided in the study metadata
record.problems: The scaling sweep uses one dataset and a fixed Qwen2.5-3b-instruct LLM. Encoder architecture changes along with parameter count, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling scores. The reported downstream scores are not language-model pretraining losses.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant Table 5 parameter-size results were omitted. The Table 6 sequence-length sweep is outside the listed versions: it varies interaction-history length, not language-model training-token count or compute.

untested.parts: Downstream performance against language-model scale or against pretraining loss; other LLM backbones; other datasets.
All of it. No held-out pretraining loss is reported.
All of it. No extrapolation is checked against larger runs.
All of it. No compute-optimal allocation is studied.
All of it. Shape changes together with size; there is no comparison at a fixed parameter count.
Loss power law for recommendation-sequence encoders. Only downstream accuracy is reported.
All of it. No fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Table 6 sequence-length sweep (32–512) for Trm++. It is declared out of scope and is recorded here under fits_no_version instead.

record.verdict_notes: The system scaled is a recommendation-sequence encoder, not a language model, and the measure is downstream accuracy, not loss. The V6 link is therefore a cross-setting analogue (T3). Only one run per size is reported, with no error bars. Architecture shape varies with size.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or language-model parameter, training-token, or compute scaling.
No prediction of much larger runs from fits on smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
Architecture details vary alongside encoder size; the study does not compare architectures at a fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or the listed alternate training regimes are tested.
Tests downstream personalized-Q&A scores across user-encoder sizes with one fixed LLM; it does not test downstream performance across general language-model scales or against pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting choices or setups for language-model scaling laws, or test whether language-model loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.stage_stated: pre-trained user encoder; evaluated after the fine-tuning stage
rows.operation_detail: Reports a scaling-law fit for performance against encoder parameter count.
rows.note: Equation is transcribed as printed; the text does not clarify the formatting.
rows.check: The printed equation drops its operator. Checking against the data points gives y = 7.53·log10(x) − 2.90 (about 65.5 at 1.2B versus 64.86 observed). This is a log-linear fit of accuracy, not a power law, and no goodness of fit is reported.

relationships.condition: Trm++ user-encoder sweep from 3.2M to 1.2B parameters, overall average score, Qwen2.5-3b-instruct backbone
relationships.reason: The overall average rises at every step, from 45.26 to 64.86 (r4, r8, r12, r16, r20, r24, r28, r32). It tracks a log-linear fit (r33).
relationships.display_finding: The overall average score increased at every size step from 45.26 to 64.86 and followed a log-linear fit.

relationships.condition: Per-task scores at individual size steps (SU at 3.2M→13M; SU and AP at 25M→57M)
relationships.reason: Some task scores stall or dip slightly as size grows (r5, r13, r14), so per-task gains are not monotonic. Architecture also changes along with size.
relationships.display_finding: Some task scores plateaued or declined slightly at larger sizes, while architecture also changed.
